name: Prestosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Triassic beds of Brazil.
• Described by Friedrich von Huene in 1942.
• Reassessed in the late 20th century.
interestingFacts: It was a large apex predator.
It had an upright limb posture.
Closely related to early crocodilians.

name: Batrachotomus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Remains found in the Kupferzell fossil site in Germany.
• Described in 1999.
• Name means 'frog slicer'.
interestingFacts: Preyed on giant amphibians.
It was a heavily built rauisuchian.
Walked on four legs but could rear up.

name: Ornithosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• First found in Scotland in the 19th century.
• Originally thought to be an ancestor to dinosaurs.
• Recognized as a pseudosuchian archosaur.
interestingFacts: It had a distinctive crocodile-like ankle.
Known for its 'bird crocodile' skull shape.
Exhibited facultative bipedalism.

name: Rutiodon
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the eastern United States.
• Named by Ebenezer Emmons in 1856.
• Extensive fossil material found in the Newark Supergroup.
interestingFacts: Nostrils were located near the eyes, not the snout tip.
Closely resembled modern gharials.
It was a phytosaur, not a true crocodile.

name: Smilosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Petrified Forest of Arizona.
• Elevated to its own genus from Machaeroprosopus.
• Known from very large skulls.
interestingFacts: Had a heavy, robust snout.
Possessed a large cranial crest.
An apex predator in aquatic environments.

name: Phytosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• First described by Georg Friedrich Jaeger in 1828.
• The first phytosaur ever named.
• Based on fragmentary remains, often considered a nomen dubium.
interestingFacts: Name translates to 'plant reptile' due to mistaken tooth interpretation.
Actually a carnivorous aquatic predator.
Gave its name to the entire group of phytosaurs.

name: Machaeroprosopus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the southwestern United States.
• Described by Maurice Mehl in 1916.
• Subject to complex taxonomic debates with other phytosaurs.
interestingFacts: Had a long, narrow snout for catching fish.
Lived in widespread river systems.
Its fossils are excellent biostratigraphic markers.

name: Leptosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils found in North America.
• Described by Case in 1922.
• Often confused or synonymized with Smilosuchus.
interestingFacts: Possessed a relatively broad skull.
Armored with bony scutes.
A widespread Late Triassic predator.

name: Redondasaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Redonda Formation of New Mexico.
• Described by Hunt and Lucas in 1993.
• One of the last known phytosaurs.
interestingFacts: Very advanced phytosaur species.
Highly adapted for aquatic ambush.
Survived until the end-Triassic extinction event.

name: Mystriosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Germany.
• Described by Eberhard Fraas in 1896.
• Further material has been found in northern Italy.
interestingFacts: Highly adapted for marine life.
Snout was extremely elongated.
Some specimens found in full marine deposits.

name: Typothorax
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the American Southwest.
• First described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1892.
• Later found to be a widely distributed aetosaur.
interestingFacts: Had extensive, broad bony armor.
Likely a slow-moving herbivore.
Armor spikes protected its neck.

name: Stagonolepis
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Lossiemouth Sandstone in Scotland.
• Initially thought to be a fish based on its scales.
• Reinterpreted as a reptile by Thomas Huxley.
interestingFacts: Had a pig-like rooting snout.
Body was heavily encased in rectangular scutes.
One of the best-understood early aetosaurs.

name: Aetosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Stubensandstein of Germany.
• Described in 1877.
• Multiple skeletons found clustered together.
interestingFacts: One of the smallest known aetosaurs.
May have exhibited gregarious behavior.
Name means 'eagle lizard'.

name: Neoaetosauroides
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils recovered from the Los Colorados Formation, Argentina.
• Described by Bonaparte in 1969.
• One of the first aetosaurs known from South America.
interestingFacts: Possessed teeth adapted for a soft diet or omnivory.
Had distinctively long limbs.
First aetosaur with well-preserved limb elements.

name: Longosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the southwestern US.
• Originally assigned to Typothorax.
• Reassigned and named after paleontologist Robert Long.
interestingFacts: Had large curved spikes on its shoulders.
A relatively robust and slow-moving aetosaur.
Common in Late Triassic fossil assemblages.

name: Gracilisuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Chañares Formation of Argentina.
• Described by Alfred Romer in 1972.
• Initially considered an early dinosaur or ornithosuchid.
interestingFacts: A very small, agile pseudosuchian.
Walked primarily on its hind legs.
Had a double row of scutes along its back.

name: Erpetosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Scotland in the 19th century.
• Later found in the eastern United States.
• Described by E.T. Newton in 1894.
interestingFacts: Very small archosaur.
Had a specialized skull suggesting an insectivorous diet.
Shares features with early crocodilians.

name: Saltoposuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Stubensandstein of Germany.
• Described by Friedrich von Huene in 1921.
• Often cited in early theories of dinosaur origins.
interestingFacts: Name translates to 'leaping crocodile'.
Very lightly built and bipedal.
Covered with thin, elongated scutes.

name: Terrestrisuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in a fissure fill in Wales.
• Described by P.M. Galton in 1984.
• Thought by some to be a juvenile Saltoposuchus.
interestingFacts: Extremely slender, greyhound-like proportions.
A fully terrestrial early crocodylomorph.
Very small, measuring around half a meter in length.

name: Hesperosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Chinle Formation of Arizona.
• Described by Colbert in 1952.
• Represents one of the earliest North American crocodylomorphs.
interestingFacts: Agile terrestrial predator.
Had distinctively long hind legs.
Likely preyed on large insects and small vertebrates.

name: Sphenosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Elliot Formation of South Africa.
• Described by Sidney Haughton in 1915.
• Holotype skull is exceptionally well-preserved.
interestingFacts: A primitive crocodylomorph with a somewhat dog-like stance.
Had a highly specialized quadrate bone.
Fully terrestrial and fast-running.

name: Protosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in Arizona in the 1930s.
• Named by Barnum Brown in 1934.
• Material also found in South Africa and Lesotho.
interestingFacts: Had short, powerful jaws.
Represented a transition toward amphibious crocodyliforms.
Heavily armored with dorsal and ventral scutes.

name: Effigia
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found at the Ghost Ranch quarry in New Mexico.
• Discovered by Sterling Nesbitt in 2006 from decades-old unprepared blocks.
• Named after Georgia O'Keeffe.
interestingFacts: A remarkable example of convergent evolution with ornithomimid dinosaurs.
Completely toothless with a beak.
Bipedal and highly cursorial.

name: Shuvosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Cooper Canyon Formation, Texas.
• Described by Sankar Chatterjee in 1993.
• Originally thought to be an early theropod dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Another beaked, toothless pseudosuchian.
Closely related to Effigia.
Demonstrates high diversity among Triassic archosaurs.

name: Poposaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Popo Agie Formation, Wyoming.
• Described by M.G. Mehl in 1915.
• Complete skeleton discovered in 2011 confirmed its bipedalism.
interestingFacts: A large bipedal pseudosuchian.
Lacked osteoderms (armor plates).
Had an upright, dinosaur-like posture.

name: Lotosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Hunan, China in the 1970s.
• Described by Zhang in 1975.
• Distinctive due to its heavy build and neural spine sail.
interestingFacts: Possessed a prominent sail on its back.
Had a toothless, beaked mouth.
Believed to have been an herbivore.

name: Arizonasaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Moenkopi Formation, Arizona.
• Described by Samuel Paul Welles in 1947.
• A complete skeleton was later described by Sterling Nesbitt.
interestingFacts: A sail-backed poposauroid.
Sail may have been used for thermoregulation or display.
Older than many other famous Triassic archosaurs.

name: Sillosuchus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Ischigualasto Formation, Argentina.
• Described by Alcober and Parrish in 1997.
• Added to the growing list of bizarre poposauroids.
interestingFacts: A very large, bipedal predator.
Part of the unique South American Triassic fauna.
Had complex cervical vertebrae.

name: Sharovipteryx
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Madygen Formation of Kyrgyzstan.
• Discovered by Aleksandr Sharov in 1971.
• Originally named Podopteryx.
interestingFacts: Had gliding membranes primarily on its hind limbs.
The only known 'hind-winged' glider.
Likely a leaper from tree to tree.

name: Longisquama
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Madygen Formation, Kyrgyzstan.
• Discovered by Aleksandr Sharov in 1969.
• Known only from the anterior half of one skeleton.
interestingFacts: Possessed incredibly long, feather-like dorsal scales.
Subject of intense debate regarding avian origins.
A highly unusual diapsid reptile.

name: Tanystropheus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils found in Europe, the Middle East, and China.
• First described by Hermann von Meyer in 1852.
• Originally thought to be a flying reptile due to long bones.
interestingFacts: Neck was longer than its body and tail combined.
Neck consisted of only 12 or 13 extremely elongated vertebrae.
Likely an ambush predator in shallow waters.

name: Macrocnemus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Besano Formation, Italy.
• Described by Nopcsa in 1930.
• Later found in Switzerland and China.
interestingFacts: A terrestrial or semi-aquatic prolacertiform.
Had long, slender hind limbs for running.
Related to Tanystropheus but with a shorter neck.

name: Dinocephalosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Guanling Formation, China.
• Described in 2004 by Li.
• A remarkable complete specimen with an embryo was described in 2017.
interestingFacts: First archosauromorph known to give live birth.
Neck had over 25 vertebrae.
Fully marine and incapable of coming on land.

name: Placodus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Muschelkalk of Germany.
• Described by Louis Agassiz in 1833.
• Originally classified as a pycnodont fish.
interestingFacts: Had thick, flat teeth for crushing shellfish.
Possessed heavy bones for ballast in water.
Looked somewhat like a marine iguana.

name: Cyamodus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Fossils found in Germany.
• Described by Hermann von Meyer in 1863.
• One of the first heavily armored placodonts known.
interestingFacts: Carried a broad, turtle-like carapace.
Carapace was divided into two distinct sections.
Bottom feeder specialized in hard-shelled prey.

name: Henodus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Gipskeuper of Germany.
• Described by von Huene in 1936.
• Found in non-marine, brackish deposits.
interestingFacts: Possessed a very boxy, flat shell.
Had a single tooth on each side, relying mostly on a beak.
May have been a filter feeder.

name: Nothosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found across Europe, North Africa, and China.
• Described by Georg zu Münster in 1834.
• One of the most abundant marine reptiles of the Triassic.
interestingFacts: A semi-oceanic predator with a long neck and tail.
Had webbed toes instead of fully formed flippers.
Probably lived similarly to modern seals.

name: Lariosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered near Lake Como, Italy.
• Described by Curioni in 1847.
• Originally recognized from small, possibly juvenile specimens.
interestingFacts: One of the smallest nothosaurs.
Forelimbs were modified into flippers, but hindlimbs retained toes.
Likely inhabited shallow coastal lagoons.

name: Ceresiosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found at Monte San Giorgio on the Swiss-Italian border.
• Described by Bernhard Peyer in 1931.
• Often debated as a species of Lariosaurus.
interestingFacts: A larger nothosaur with highly adapted flippers.
Excellent swimmer due to hyperphalangy in its digits.
A transitional form toward plesiosaurs.

name: Pistosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Muschelkalk of Germany.
• Described by Christian Erich Hermann von Meyer in 1839.
• Represented by very few well-preserved specimens.
interestingFacts: Had a stiff spine and plesiosaur-like skull.
A key transitional fossil linking nothosaurs and plesiosaurs.
Fully marine, utilizing flipper-based locomotion.

name: Simosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in the Muschelkalk deposits of Germany.
• Described in the 19th century.
• Skulls are commonly found, but complete skeletons are rare.
interestingFacts: Had a blunt, short snout unlike other nothosaurs.
Probably fed on hard-shelled organisms.
Lack of typical pointed teeth suggests a specialized diet.

name: Mixosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in marine deposits worldwide.
• Described by George H. Baur in 1887.
• Represents one of the most common early ichthyosaurs.
interestingFacts: A transitional ichthyosaur with a straight tail.
Retained a distinct neck, unlike later forms.
Small and agile marine predator.

name: Besanosaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered at the Besano formation in Italy in 1993.
• Described by Dal Sasso and Pinna in 1996.
• The holotype specimen was pregnant.
interestingFacts: A large shastasaurid ichthyosaur.
Lacked a dorsal fin.
Gave birth to live young tail-first, like modern cetaceans.

name: Shastasaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• First discovered in Mount Shasta, California.
• Described by Merriam in 1895.
• Later found in China and Canada.
interestingFacts: One of the largest marine reptiles ever.
S. sikanniensis reached over 20 meters in length.
Likely a suction feeder lacking typical teeth.

name: Guanlingsaurus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered in Guanling County, Guizhou, China.
• Described by Yin et al. in 2000.
• Often considered a species of Shastasaurus.
interestingFacts: Characterized by a uniquely short and toothless snout.
An enormous marine reptile.
Adapted for suction feeding on soft-bodied cephalopods.

name: Eudimorphodon
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Discovered near Bergamo, Italy in 1973.
• Described by Rocco Zambelli.
• One of the oldest known pterosaurs.
interestingFacts: Possessed complex, multi-cusped teeth.
Had a diamond-shaped flap of skin at the end of its long tail.
Likely a piscivore (fish-eater).

name: Preondactylus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory:
• Found in the Preone valley in Italy in 1982.
• Described by Rupert Wild in 1984.
• Specimen was discovered in a piece of bituminous limestone.
interestingFacts: One of the most basal pterosaurs.
Had single-cusped teeth unlike Eudimorphodon.
Wingspan was less than half a meter.

name: Austriadactylus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the 20th century.
interestingFacts: Austriadactylus is an important Triassic species.
It tells us about early ecosystems.

name: Caviramus
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the 20th century.
interestingFacts: Caviramus is an important Triassic species.
It tells us about early ecosystems.

name: Campylognathoides
dietDetails: Consumed what was available in its ecosystem.
discoveryHistory: Discovered in the 20th century.
interestingFacts: Campylognathoides is an important Triassic species.
It tells us about early ecosystems.
